claim: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can be damaged during mammalian development.
source: Dangerous damage to mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can be ameliorated during mammalian development through a highly debated mechanism called the mtDNA bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about mtDNA damage during development.

claim: The mtDNA bottleneck is a mechanism that can ameliorate dangerous mtDNA damage during mammalian development.
source: Dangerous damage to mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can be ameliorated during mammalian development through a highly debated mechanism called the mtDNA bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known mechanism.

claim: The mtDNA bottleneck mechanism is highly debated.
source: Dangerous damage to mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can be ameliorated during mammalian development through a highly debated mechanism called the mtDNA bottleneck.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the mechanism is 'highly debated'.

claim: Uncertainty surrounding the mtDNA bottleneck process limits the ability to address inherited mtDNA diseases.
source: Uncertainty surrounding this process limits our ability to address inherited mtDNA diseases.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the uncertainty in the abstract.

claim: A combination of binomial partitioning of mtDNAs at cell divisions and random mtDNA turnover has the most statistical support as the bottleneck mechanism.
source: Using approximate Bayesian computation and mouse data, we find most statistical support for a combination of binomial partitioning of mtDNAs at cell divisions and random mtDNA turnover, meaning that the debated exact magnitude of mtDNA copy number depletion is flexible.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by ABC analysis of mouse data.

claim: The exact magnitude of mtDNA copy number depletion during the bottleneck is flexible.
source: Using approximate Bayesian computation and mouse data, we find most statistical support for a combination of binomial partitioning of mtDNAs at cell divisions and random mtDNA turnover, meaning that the debated exact magnitude of mtDNA copy number depletion is flexible.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the statistical analysis in the abstract.

claim: New experimental measurements from a wild-derived mtDNA pairing in mice confirm the theoretical predictions of the BDP model.
source: New experimental measurements from a wild-derived mtDNA pairing in mice confirm the theoretical predictions of this model.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondria are vital energy-producing organelles within eukaryotic cells.
source: Mitochondria are vital energy-producing organelles within eukaryotic cells, possessing genomes (mitochondrial DNA, mtDNA) that replicate, degrade and develop mutations (Rand, 2001; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondria possess genomes (mtDNA) that replicate, degrade and develop mutations.
source: Mitochondria are vital energy-producing organelles within eukaryotic cells, possessing genomes (mitochondrial DNA, mtDNA) that replicate, degrade and develop mutations (Rand, 2001; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: MtDNA mutations have been implicated in numerous pathologies including fatal inherited diseases and ageing.
source: MtDNA mutations have been implicated in numerous pathologies including fatal inherited diseases and ageing (Lightowlers et al., 1997; Wallace, 1999; Poulton et al., 2009; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Combatting the buildup of mtDNA mutations is of paramount importance in ensuring an organism's survival.
source: Combatting the buildup of mtDNA mutations is of paramount importance in ensuring an organism's survival.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the pathological effects of mtDNA mutations.

claim: Substantial recent medical, experimental, and media attention has focused on methods to remove or prevent the inheritance of mutated mtDNA in humans.
source: Substantial recent medical, experimental, and media attention has focused on methods to remove (Bacman et al., 2013) or prevent the inheritance of (Bredenoord et al., 2008; Poulton et al., 2009; Craven et al., 2010; Poulton et al., 2010; Burgstaller et al., 2015) mutated mtDNA in humans.
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Bottlenecking is a developmental process through which organisms may ameliorate mtDNA damage that builds up through a lifetime.
source: One means by which organisms may ameliorate the mtDNA damage that builds up through a lifetime is through a developmental process known as bottlenecking.
evidence: This is stated as an established concept in the introduction.

claim: Immediately after fertilisation, a single oocyte may contain >10^5 individual mtDNAs.
source: Immediately after fertilisation, a single oocyte (which may contain >105 individual mtDNAs) may have a nonzero mtDNA mutant load or heteroplasmy (the proportion of mutant mtDNA in the cell).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about oocyte mtDNA content.

claim: Heteroplasmy is the proportion of mutant mtDNA in a cell.
source: Immediately after fertilisation, a single oocyte (which may contain >105 individual mtDNAs) may have a nonzero mtDNA mutant load or heteroplasmy (the proportion of mutant mtDNA in the cell).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: As the number of cells in the developing organism increases, the intercellular population acquires an associated heteroplasmy variance.
source: As the number of cells in the developing organism increases, the intercellular population then acquires an associated heteroplasmy variance, that is, the variance in mutant load across the population of cells (Figure 1A), allowing removal of cells with high heteroplasmy and retention of cells with low heteroplasmy.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Heteroplasmy variance allows removal of cells with high heteroplasmy and retention of cells with low heteroplasmy.
source: As the number of cells in the developing organism increases, the intercellular population then acquires an associated heteroplasmy variance, that is, the variance in mutant load across the population of cells (Figure 1A), allowing removal of cells with high heteroplasmy and retention of cells with low heteroplasmy.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of heteroplasmy variance development.

claim: Intense and sustained debate exists as to the mechanism by which the increase of heteroplasmy variance occurs.
source: Intense and sustained debate exists as to the mechanism by which this increase of heteroplasmy variance occurs.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the current state of the field.

claim: During development, the copy number of mtDNA per cell in the germ cell line drops dramatically to ~10^2 in mice.
source: Several experimental results in mice suggest that, during development, the copy number of mtDNA per cell in the germ cell line drops dramatically to ∼102, reducing the effective population size of mitochondrial genomes (Cree et al., 2008; Wai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to experimental studies.

claim: One postulated bottlenecking mechanism is that low mtDNA population size accelerates genetic drift and increases cell-to-cell heteroplasmy variance.
source: One postulated bottlenecking mechanism is that this low population size accelerates genetic drift and so increases the cell-to-cell heteroplasmy variance (Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Aiken et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008; Wonnapinij et al., 2010), which was first observed to generally increase from primordial germ cells through primary oocytes to mature oocytes (Jenuth et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Heteroplasmy variance was first observed to generally increase from primordial germ cells through primary oocytes to mature oocytes.
source: One postulated bottlenecking mechanism is that this low population size accelerates genetic drift and so increases the cell-to-cell heteroplasmy variance (Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Aiken et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008; Wonnapinij et al., 2010), which was first observed to generally increase from primordial germ cells through primary oocytes to mature oocytes (Jenuth et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original observation.

claim: Independent experimental evidence suggests that heteroplasmy variance increases negligibly during mtDNA copy number reduction.
source: However, independent experimental evidence (Wai et al., 2008) suggests that heteroplasmy variance increases negligibly during this copy number reduction, though this interpretation has been debated (Samuels et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to experimental evidence and subsequent debate.

claim: Heteroplasmy variance rises during folliculogenesis, after the mtDNA copy number minimum has been passed.
source: Wai et al. (2008) shows heteroplasmy variance rising during folliculogenesis, after the mtDNA copy number minimum has been passed.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to experimental evidence.

claim: Conflicting experimental results support a picture where heteroplasmy variance increases with a less pronounced decrease in mtDNA copy number (minimum >10^3 in mice) solely through random effects associated with partitioning at cell divisions.
source: In yet another picture, supported by conflicting experimental results (Cao et al., 2007, 2009), heteroplasmy variance increases with a less pronounced decrease in mtDNA copy number (a minimum copy number >103 in mice), solely through random effects associated with partitioning at cell divisions.
evidence: This is stated with citations to experimental studies.

claim: A consensus on the bottleneck mechanism is yet to be reached.
source: Clearly a consensus on this important mechanism is yet to be reached.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the conflicting evidence presented.

claim: Important existing theoretical work on the bottleneck has assumed a particular underlying mechanism or derived statistics without explicitly considering changing mtDNA population size or the discrete nature of the mtDNA population.
source: Important existing theoretical work on modelling the bottleneck has assumed a particular underlying mechanism (Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Wolff et al., 2011) or derived statistics of mtDNA populations (Chinnery and Samuels, 1999; Elson et al., 2001; Wonnapinij et al., 2008, 2010) without explicitly considering changing mtDNA population size, or the discrete nature of the mtDNA population: effects which may powerfully affect mtDNA statistics.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of existing theoretical work with supporting citations.

claim: Changing mtDNA population size and the discrete nature of the mtDNA population may powerfully affect mtDNA statistics.
source: Important existing theoretical work on modelling the bottleneck has assumed a particular underlying mechanism (Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Wolff et al., 2011) or derived statistics of mtDNA populations (Chinnery and Samuels, 1999; Elson et al., 2001; Wonnapinij et al., 2008, 2010) without explicitly considering changing mtDNA population size, or the discrete nature of the mtDNA population: effects which may powerfully affect mtDNA statistics.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the current study's approach.

claim: A 'bottom-up' physical description of mtDNA as populations of individual, discrete elements subject to replication and degradation is necessary to capture the effects of changing population size and discrete nature.
source: To capture these effects it is necessary to employ a 'bottom-up' physical description of mtDNA as populations of individual, discrete elements subject to replication and degradation, as in, for example, (Chinnery and Samuels, 1999) and (Capps et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement with supporting citations.

claim: Previous simulation work has not allowed for the wide variety of replication and partitioning dynamics proposed in the literature.
source: While previous simulation work (Cree et al., 2008; Poovathingal et al., 2009) has taken such a philosophy with specific model assumptions, we are not aware of such a study allowing for the wide variety of replication and partitioning dynamics proposed in the literature; we further note that replication-degradation-partitioning mtDNA models are yet to be fully described analytically.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Replication-degradation-partitioning mtDNA models are yet to be fully described analytically.
source: While previous simulation work (Cree et al., 2008; Poovathingal et al., 2009) has taken such a philosophy with specific model assumptions, we are not aware of such a study allowing for the wide variety of replication and partitioning dynamics proposed in the literature; we further note that replication-degradation-partitioning mtDNA models are yet to be fully described analytically.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: There is no general quantitative framework under which different proposed bottleneck mechanisms can be statistically compared given extant data.
source: Nor is there a general quantitative framework under which different proposed bottleneck mechanisms can be statistically compared given extant data (although statistical analyses focusing on particular mechanisms and individual sets of experimental results have been used throughout the literature, for example, using a Bayesian approach under a particular bottleneck model to infer model bottleneck size [Marchington et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature with a citation to related work.

claim: The general model for the bottleneck can describe the Cree and Wai (a) mechanisms through the BDP mechanism.
source: The Wai (a) mechanism and the Cree model can both be addressed in the same mechanistic framework (with potentially different parameterisations): if the rate of random replication in the Cree model is sufficiently low during folliculogenesis, only a subset of mtDNAs will be actively replicating at any given time during this period, thus recapitulating the Wai (a) mechanism (see Appendix 1). We will henceforth combine discussion of the Wai (a) and Cree mechanisms into what we term the birth-death-partition (BDP) mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical result from the model construction.

claim: The BDP model has the most statistical support given experimental measurements.
source: Figure 2B clearly shows that as the ABC threshold is decreased, requiring closer agreement between the distributions of simulated and experimental data, the posterior probability of the BDP model increases, to dramatically exceed those of the other models.
evidence: This is stated as a result from ABC model selection and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The BDP model is capable of providing the best explanation of experimental data.
source: This increase indicates that the BDP model is the most statistically supported, and capable of providing the best explanation of experimental data (which can be inutitively seen from the trajectories in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ABC analysis and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: ABC model selection automatically takes model complexity into account.
source: We note that ABC model selection automatically takes model complexity into account, and conclude that the BDP mechanism is the best supported proposed mechanism for the bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the ABC method.

claim: The BDP model produces increasing variance both due to early cell division stochasticity and later random turnover.
source: Briefly, this result arises because the BDP model produces increasing variance both due to early cell division stochasticity and later random turnover.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the model's success.

claim: The Cao model alone only increases variance in early development when cell divisions are occurring.
source: By contrast, the Cao model alone only increases variance in early development when cell divisions are occurring.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Cao model.

claim: The Wai (b) model alone only increases variance at a single time point during folliculogenesis.
source: The Wai (b) model alone similarly only increases variance at a single time point (later, during folliculogenesis).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Wai (b) model.

claim: The BDP model results in the observation of only a subset of replicating mtDNAs over the timeframe corresponding to experimental results from Wai et al. (2008).
source: In Appendix 1, we show that the BDP model also results in the observation of only a subset of replicating mtDNAs over the timeframe corresponding to these experimental results.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in the Appendix.

claim: The Wai (b) mechanism requires the replication of <1% of mtDNAs during folliculogenesis to yield reasonable heteroplasmy variance increases.
source: We also note the mathematical observation that the Wai (b) mechanism requires the replication of <1% of mtDNAs during folliculogenesis to yield reasonable heteroplasmy variance increases (Figure 2A shows the optimal case with α = 0.006; optimal fits to data generally show 0.005 < α < 0.01), and the proportions of loci visible in Wai et al. (2008) are substantially higher than this required 1% value.
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical observation from model fitting shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Substantial flexibility exists in the magnitude of the copy number minimum, with observed heteroplasmy variance resulting from a range of bottleneck sizes from ~200 to >10^3.
source: Substantial flexibility exists in the magnitude of the copy number minimum, illustrating that observed heteroplasmy variance can result from a range of bottleneck sizes from ∼200 to >103; going some way towards reconciling the conflict between Cao et al. (2007) and Cao et al. (2009) and Cree et al. (2008) and Wai et al. (2008).
evidence: This is stated as a result from parametric inference shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The BDP mechanism predicts that heteroplasmy variance acquires an intermediate value as a result of the copy number bottleneck, then continues to increase due to mtDNA turnover in later development.
source: Key among these are the prediction that heteroplasmy variance acquires an intermediate (nonzero, but not maximal) value as a result of the copy number bottleneck, then continues to increase due to mtDNA turnover in later development.
evidence: This is stated as a key prediction of the BDP model.

claim: New experimental measurements of germline heteroplasmy variance in HB mice show that variance around birth is low but non-zero, subsequently increasing with time.
source: Figure 4A shows these V′(h) measurements. The qualitative behaviour predicted by the BDP mechanism is clearly visible: variance around birth (after the copy number bottleneck) is low but non-zero, subsequently increasing with time.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The BDP mechanism experiences by far the strongest statistical support in the genetically different HB system.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, the BDP mechanism again experiences by far the strongest statistical support in this genetically different system.
evidence: This is stated as a result from ABC model selection shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No withheld datasets show significant support against the predicted heteroplasmy distribution (Anderson-Darling test, p < 0.05).
source: Insets show, in untransformed space, distributions of the withheld heteroplasmy measurements (blue) compared to parameterised predictions (red); no withheld datasets show significant support against the predicted distribution (Anderson-Darling test, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from testing the model predictions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The BDP model yields analytic solutions for the values of all genetic properties of interest.
source: Importantly, the BDP model yields analytic solutions for the values of all genetic properties of interest, using tools from stochastic processes (detail in 'Materials and methods' and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical result of the study.

claim: Analytic results provide an excellent match to the numeric results of stochastic simulation across all BDP model parameterisations.
source: In Figure 2A we illustrate that these analytic results provide an excellent match to the numeric results of stochastic simulation, a result that holds across all BDP model parameterisations.
evidence: This is stated as a validation result shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Increasing mtDNA turnover increases heteroplasmy variance.
source: This increased mtDNA turnover increases the heteroplasmy variance (see Figure 5A) due to the increased variability in mtDNA copy number from the underlying random processes occurring at increased rates.
evidence: This is stated as a result from model perturbation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing mtDNA degradation without increasing replication increases heteroplasmy variance and decreases overall mtDNA copy number.
source: We find that increasing mtDNA degradation ν without increasing λ also increases heteroplasmy variance, in addition to decreasing the overall mtDNA copy number (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model perturbation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: An artificial intervention increasing mitochondrial degradation may generally be expected to increase heteroplasmy variance during development.
source: These results suggest that an artificial intervention increasing mitochondrial degradation may generally be expected to increase heteroplasmy variance during development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the perturbation analysis.

claim: Mitochondrial degradation may represent a potential clinical target to address the inheritance of mtDNA disease.
source: For this reason, we speculate that mitochondrial degradation may represent a potential clinical target to address the inheritance of mtDNA disease (more detail in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the perturbation analysis.

claim: Pathological symptoms of mtDNA diseases usually manifest when heteroplasmy in a tissue exceeds a certain threshold value.
source: A key feature of mtDNA diseases is that pathological symptoms usually manifest when heteroplasmy in a tissue exceeds a certain threshold value, with few or no symptoms manifested below this threshold (Rossignol et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The probability and timescale with which cellular heteroplasmy may be expected to exceed a given value is a quantity of key interest in clinical planning of mtDNA disease strategies.
source: The probability and timescale with which cellular heteroplasmy may be expected to exceed a given value is thus a quantity of key interest in clinical planning of mtDNA disease strategies.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the threshold effect.

claim: The theory allows general quantitative calculation of the probability and timescale that any given heteroplasmy threshold will be exceeded, given knowledge of the initial heteroplasmy.
source: Our theory thus allows general quantitative calculation of the probability (and timescale) that any given heteroplasmy threshold will be exceeded, given knowledge of the initial (or early) heteroplasmy.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the developed theory.

claim: The increasing heteroplasmy variance through development means that substantially greater uncertainty is associated with heteroplasmy values inferred using measurements taken at later times.
source: The increasing heteroplasmy variance through development means that substantially greater uncertainty is associated with heteroplasmy values inferred using measurements taken at later times.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the preimplantation sampling analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The bottleneck is most likely manifest through stochastic mtDNA dynamics and partitioning, with increased random turnover later during development.
source: We have used a general stochastic model and approximate Bayesian computation with the available experimental data on developmental mtDNA dynamics to show that the bottleneck is most likely manifest through stochastic mtDNA dynamics and partitioning, with increased random turnover later during development, a mechanism which we can describe exactly and analytically (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study, summarized in Figure 6.

claim: The bottom-up construction of the model from physical first principles increases the flexibility and generality of the model.
source: We emphasise that the bottom-up construction of our model from physical first principles both increases the flexibility and generality of our model, allowing different mechanisms to be compared together, and providing information on mtDNA dynamics throughout development rather than estimating an overall effect.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the modeling approach.

claim: The model's ability to recapitulate the wide range of extant experimental measurements suggests that its study may yield useful insights into the effects of different treatments and perturbations on the bottleneck.
source: We note that even though our model cannot represent the full microscopic truth underlying the mtDNA bottleneck, its ability to recapitulate the wide range of extant experimental measurements suggest that its study may yield useful insights into the effects of different treatments and perturbations on the bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for the model's utility despite its limitations.

claim: A key debate in the literature has focused on the magnitude of the bottleneck.
source: A key debate in the literature has focussed on the magnitude of the bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the literature.

claim: Some studies have observed a depletion of mtDNA copy number during the bottleneck to minima around several hundred.
source: Some studies (Aiken et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008) have observed a depletion of mtDNA copy number during the bottleneck to minima around several hundred; other studies (Cao et al., 2007, 2009) have observed that mtDNA copy number remains >103.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Other studies have observed that mtDNA copy number remains >10^3 during the bottleneck.
source: Some studies (Aiken et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008) have observed a depletion of mtDNA copy number during the bottleneck to minima around several hundred; other studies (Cao et al., 2007, 2009) have observed that mtDNA copy number remains >103.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Observed increases in heteroplasmy variance can be achieved across a range of potential minimal mtDNA copy numbers.
source: Our study shows that observed increases in heteroplasmy variance (Jenuth et al., 1996; Wai et al., 2008) can be achieved across this range of potential minimal mtDNA copy numbers, meaning that the much-debated magnitude of mtDNA copy number reduction is not the sole critical feature of the bottleneck, in agreement with arguments from Cao et al. (2007, 2009); Wai et al. (2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study with supporting citations.

claim: The much-debated magnitude of mtDNA copy number reduction is not the sole critical feature of the bottleneck.
source: Our study shows that observed increases in heteroplasmy variance (Jenuth et al., 1996; Wai et al., 2008) can be achieved across this range of potential minimal mtDNA copy numbers, meaning that the much-debated magnitude of mtDNA copy number reduction is not the sole critical feature of the bottleneck, in agreement with arguments from Cao et al. (2007, 2009); Wai et al. (2008).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study with supporting citations.

claim: The role of stochastic mtDNA dynamics can play a key role in determining heteroplasmy variance without additional mechanistic details.
source: We find that the role of stochastic mtDNA dynamics can play a key role in determining heteroplasmy variance without additional mechanistic details, in keeping with approaches proposed by Cree et al. (2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study with a supporting citation.

claim: The mechanism with the most statistical support is consistent with aspects from all existing proposals in the literature.
source: The mechanism with the most statistical support is thus consistent with aspects from all existing proposals in the literature.
evidence: This is stated as a synthesis of the findings.

claim: The BDP model is the individually most likely mechanism and capable of producing experimentally observed heteroplasmy behaviour.
source: We have shown that, of the models proposed in the literature, a BDP model, proposed after Cree et al. (2008) and compatible with an interpretation of Wai et al. (2008), is the individually most likely mechanism, and capable of producing experimentally observed heteroplasmy behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion with supporting citations.

claim: Hybrid mechanisms, where BDP dominates but small contributions from other mechanisms provide perturbations, cannot be discounted given current experimental evidence.
source: We cannot, given current experimental evidence, discount hybrid mechanisms, where BDP dominates the population dynamics but small contributions from other mechanisms provide perturbations to this behaviour, and propose experiments to conclusively distinguish between these cases (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current conclusions.

claim: The expected statistics of mtDNA populations undergoing inheritance of heteroplasmic mtDNA clusters is very similar to those undergoing binomial partitioning of mtDNAs.
source: As the expected statistics of mtDNA populations undergoing inheritance of heteroplasmic mtDNA clusters is very similar to those undergoing binomial partitioning of mtDNAs (see Appendix 1), the inheritance of heteroplasmic nucleoids (as opposed to individual mtDNAs) is not excluded by our findings, though other recent experimental evidence suggests that this situation may be unlikely (Poe et al., 2010; Jakobs and Wurm, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical result with supporting citations.

claim: The most likely situation may involve the partitioning of individual organelles, containing a mixture of homoplasmic nucleoids of characteristic size <2.
source: We contend that the most likely situation may involve the partitioning of individual organelles, containing a mixture of homoplasmic nucleoids of characteristic size <2.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' interpretation of the findings.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics (fission and fusion) likely play a role in determining natural mtDNA turnover.
source: As mentioned in the model description, it is likely that mitochondrial dynamics (fission and fusion of mitochondria) (Detmer and Chan, 2007) play a role in determining natural mtDNA turnover, and particularly mtDNA turnover in the presence of pathological mutations (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012), through the mechanism of mitochondrial quality control (Twig et al., 2008; Twig and Shirihai, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics may influence the elements of partitioning through changes in the connectivity of the mitochondrial network.
source: Mitochondrial dynamics may also influence the elements of partitioning, through changes in the connectivity of the mitochondrial network.
evidence: This is stated as a potential mechanism.

claim: Physical parameters of mtDNA replication, degradation, and partitioning are expected to be the key determinants of heteroplasmy statistics through development.
source: These physical parameters, as opposed to the more microscopic details of mitochondrial dynamics, are expected to be the key determinants of heteroplasmy statistics through development.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for the modeling approach.

claim: Observation of similar dynamics in salmon points towards the bottleneck being a conserved mechanism in vertebrates.
source: Observation of similar dynamics in salmon (Wolff et al., 2011) points towards the bottleneck being a conserved mechanism in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Results in mice are broadly consistent with findings from recent experiments in other organisms, suggesting that in primates and humans, heteroplasmy variance may increase at early developmental stages.
source: We also note that our results in mice are broadly consistent with findings from recent experiments in other organisms, suggesting that in primates and humans, heteroplasmy variance may increase at early developmental stages (Monnot et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012), and that partitioning of mitochondria is binomial in HeLa cells (Johnston et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Partitioning of mitochondria is binomial in HeLa cells.
source: We also note that our results in mice are broadly consistent with findings from recent experiments in other organisms, suggesting that in primates and humans, heteroplasmy variance may increase at early developmental stages (Monnot et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012), and that partitioning of mitochondria is binomial in HeLa cells (Johnston et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Results of a recent study of human preimplantation sampling found that earlier measurements provided strong predictive power of mean heteroplasmy, about which substantial variation was recorded in the offspring.
source: We note that the results of a recent study of human preimplantation sampling (Treff et al., 2012) found that earlier measurements provided strong predictive power of mean heteroplasmy, about which substantial variation was recorded in the offspring—both of which results are consistent with the application of our model to theoretical sampling considerations.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The m.3243A>G mutation in humans both increases mtDNA copy number during development and displays a less pronounced increase of heteroplasmy variance than other mutations.
source: In addition, recent observations that the m.3243A > G mutation in humans both increases mtDNA copy number during development (Monnot et al., 2013), and displays a less pronounced increase of heteroplasmy variance (Monnot et al., 2011) than other mutations, are consistent with the link between heteroplasmy variance and mtDNA copy number in our theory.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The observations about the m.3243A>G mutation are consistent with the link between heteroplasmy variance and mtDNA copy number in the theory.
source: In addition, recent observations that the m.3243A > G mutation in humans both increases mtDNA copy number during development (Monnot et al., 2013), and displays a less pronounced increase of heteroplasmy variance (Monnot et al., 2011) than other mutations, are consistent with the link between heteroplasmy variance and mtDNA copy number in our theory.
evidence: This is stated as a consistency check with the theory.

claim: The combination of modern stochastic and statistical treatments provides a generalisable and powerful way to recapitulate experimental data and rigorously deduce underlying biological mechanisms.
source: The combination of modern stochastic and statistical treatments that we have employed provides a generalisable and powerful way to recapitulate experimental data and rigorously deduce underlying biological mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological conclusion.

claim: The detailed elucidation of the bottleneck allows proposal of further experimental methodology to address current unknowns in the theory.
source: Our detailed elucidation of the bottleneck allows us to propose further experimental methodology to address the current unknowns in our theory, including the specifics of mtDNA partitioning at cell division and the roles of selective differences between mtDNA types; importantly, we also propose a strategy to investigate our claim that our most supported model is compatible with the subset-replication picture of mtDNA dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: The theoretical foundation for mtDNA dynamics allows increased quantitative rigour in the predictions and strategies involved in mtDNA disease therapies.
source: Finally, we believe that the theoretical foundation for mtDNA dynamics that we have produced allows increased quantitative rigour in the predictions and strategies involved in mtDNA disease therapies, illustrated by the above application of our theory to problems in mtDNA sampling strategies, disease onset timescales, and interventions to increase the power of the bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the theory.

claim: The general model represents individual mtDNAs as elements which replicate and degrade either randomly or deterministically according to the model parameterisation.
source: Our 'bottom-up' model represents individual mtDNAs as elements which replicate and degrade either randomly or deterministically according to the model parameterisation.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model.

claim: It is often a single mutant genotype that dominates the non-wildtype mtDNA population of a cell.
source: Consonant with experimental studies showing that it is often a single mutant genotype that dominates the non-wildtype mtDNA population of a cell (Khrapko et al., 1999), we consider two mtDNA types (wildtype and mutant), though our model can readily be extended to more mtDNA types.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The model considers two mtDNA types (wildtype and mutant), though it can readily be extended to more mtDNA types.
source: Consonant with experimental studies showing that it is often a single mutant genotype that dominates the non-wildtype mtDNA population of a cell (Khrapko et al., 1999), we consider two mtDNA types (wildtype and mutant), though our model can readily be extended to more mtDNA types.
evidence: This is stated as a model design choice.

claim: Individual mtDNAs are capable of replication and degradation, with rates denoted λ and ν respectively.
source: Individual mtDNAs are capable of replication and degradation, with rates denoted λ and ν respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a model feature.

claim: A parameter S determines whether replication and degradation events are deterministic (S=0) or Poisson processes (S=1).
source: According to a binary categorical parameter S, these events may be deterministic (S = 0; the mtDNA population replicates and degrades by a fixed amount per unit time) or Poisson processes (S = 1; each individual mtDNA randomly replicates and degrades with average rates λ and ν).
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter.

claim: A parameter α controls the proportion of mtDNAs capable of replication.
source: A parameter α controls the proportion of mtDNAs capable of replication: α = 1 allows all mtDNAs to replicate throughout development, α < 1 enforces a subset proportion α of replicating mtDNAs a time cutoff T after conception.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter.

claim: When α = 1, all mtDNAs may replicate throughout development.
source: A parameter α controls the proportion of mtDNAs capable of replication: α = 1 allows all mtDNAs to replicate throughout development, α < 1 enforces a subset proportion α of replicating mtDNAs a time cutoff T after conception.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter specification.

claim: When α < 1, replication of a subset proportion α of mtDNAs is enforced at time cutoff T after conception.
source: A parameter α controls the proportion of mtDNAs capable of replication: α = 1 allows all mtDNAs to replicate throughout development, α < 1 enforces a subset proportion α of replicating mtDNAs a time cutoff T after conception.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter specification.

claim: A parameter c (cluster size) dictates the partitioning of mtDNAs at cell divisions.
source: A parameter c (cluster size; a non-negative integer) dictates the partitioning of mtDNAs at cell divisions.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter.

claim: When c = 0, partitioning is deterministic, so each daughter cell receives exactly half of its parent's mtDNA.
source: When c = 0, partitioning is deterministic, so each daughter cell receives exactly half of its parent's mtDNA.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter specification.

claim: When c = 1, partitioning is binomial: each mtDNA has a 50% chance of being inherited by either daughter cell.
source: When c = 1, partitioning is binomial: each mtDNA has a 50% chance of being inherited by either daughter cell.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter specification.

claim: When c > 1, the parent cell's mtDNAs are grouped in clusters of size c before division, and each cluster is then partitioned binomially.
source: When c > 1, the parent cell's mtDNAs are grouped in clusters of size c before division. Each cluster is then partitioned binomially, with a 50% chance of being inherited by either daughter cell.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter specification.

claim: The model includes six different dynamic phases throughout development, each with different rates of replication and degradation.
source: We allow six different phases, with the first two fixed as cycling phases with the above doubling times, and the final phase fixed to include no mtDNA replication (representing the stable, final occyte state).
evidence: This is stated as a model design feature.

claim: The first two phases are fixed as cycling phases with specified doubling times.
source: We allow six different phases, with the first two fixed as cycling phases with the above doubling times, and the final phase fixed to include no mtDNA replication (representing the stable, final occyte state).
evidence: This is stated as a model design feature.

claim: The final phase is fixed to include no mtDNA replication, representing the stable, final oocyte state.
source: We allow six different phases, with the first two fixed as cycling phases with the above doubling times, and the final phase fixed to include no mtDNA replication (representing the stable, final occyte state).
evidence: This is stated as a model design feature.

claim: The initial conditions of the model involve an initial mtDNA copy number m0 and an initial heteroplasmy h0.
source: The initial conditions of our model involve an initial mtDNA copy number m0 (the total number of mtDNAs in the fertilised oocyte) and an initial heteroplasmy h0 (the fraction of these mtDNAs that are mutated).
evidence: This is stated as a model specification.

claim: Data on cell doubling times in the mouse germ line suggests that doubling times start with an interval of every 7 hr, then after around 8.5 dpc increase to 16 hr, before the onset of a quiescent regime around 13.5 dpc.
source: Data on cell doubling times in the mouse germ line is taken from Lawson and Hage (1994), suggesting that doubling times start with an interval of every 7 hr, then after around 8.5 days post conception (dpc) increase to 16 hr, before the onset of a quiescent regime around 13.5 dpc (roughly consistent with the estimate of ∼25 divisions between generations in the female mouse germ line [Drost and Lee, 1995]).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The cell doubling time data is roughly consistent with the estimate of ~25 divisions between generations in the female mouse germ line.
source: Data on cell doubling times in the mouse germ line is taken from Lawson and Hage (1994), suggesting that doubling times start with an interval of every 7 hr, then after around 8.5 days post conception (dpc) increase to 16 hr, before the onset of a quiescent regime around 13.5 dpc (roughly consistent with the estimate of ∼25 divisions between generations in the female mouse germ line [Drost and Lee, 1995]).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Gillespie algorithms (stochastic simulation algorithms) are used to explore the behaviour of the model for a given parameterisation.
source: We use Gillespie algorithms, also known as stochastic simulation algorithms (Gillespie, 1977), to explore the behaviour of our model of the bottlenecking process for a given parameterisation.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice with a supporting citation.

claim: For a given model parameterisation, the Gillespie algorithm is used to simulate an ensemble of 10^3 possible realisations of the time evolution of mtDNA content.
source: For a given model parameterisation, the Gillespie algorithm is used to simulate an ensemble of 103 possible realisations of the time evolution of mtDNA content, and the statistics of this ensemble are recorded.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological procedure.

claim: Heteroplasmic mice were obtained from a heteroplasmic mouse line (HB) created previously by ooplasmic transfer.
source: Heteroplasmic mice were obtained from a heteroplasmic mouse line (HB) we created previously by ooplasmic transfer (Burgstaller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental method with a supporting citation.

claim: The HB mouse line contains the nuclear DNA of the C57BL/6N mouse, and mtDNAs both of C57BL/6N and a wild-derived house mouse.
source: This mouse line contains the nuclear DNA of the C57BL/6N mouse, and mtDNAs both of C57BL/6N and a wild-derived house mouse.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental model.

claim: Both mtDNA variants in the HB mouse line belong to the same subspecies, Mus musculus domesticus.
source: Both mtDNA variants belong to the same subspecies, Mus musculus domesticus.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental model.

claim: Heteroplasmy quantification was performed by ARMS-qPCR, an established method in the field.
source: Heteroplasmy quantification was performed by ARMS-qPCR, an established method in the field (Steinborn et al., 2000; Paull et al., 2013; Tachibana et al., 2013), as described in Burgstaller et al. (2014).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental method with supporting citations.

claim: The study was conducted according to MIQE (minimum information for publication of quantitative real-time PCR experiments) guidelines.
source: The study was conducted according to MIQE (minimum information for publication of quantitative real-time PCR experiments) guidelines (Bustin et al., 2009; Burgstaller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental standard with supporting citations.

claim: In the BDP model, processes within a cell cycle constitute a birth-death process which can be solved using generating functions.
source: In the BDP model, processes within a cell cycle constitute a birth-death process which can be solved using generating functions (Gardiner, 1985).
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical approach with a supporting citation.

claim: For binomial partitioning, the generating function for the system after an arbitrary number of divisions has a recursive structure and an analytic solution can be obtained through solving a Riccati recurrence relation.
source: For binomial partitioning, the generating function for the system after an arbitrary number of divisions has a recursive structure (Rausenberger and Kollmann, 2008; Johnston and Jones, 2015) and an analytic solution can be obtained through solving a Riccati recurrence relation.
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical result with supporting citations.

claim: The reasoning for solving the BDP model extends to different phases of replication and degradation, allowing an exact generating function to be constructed for an arbitrary point in the bottleneck.
source: This reasoning also extends to the different phases of replication and degradation, allowing an exact generating function to be constructed for an arbitrary point in the bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical result.

claim: Derivatives of the generating function are used to obtain moments of the distributions of interest.
source: Derivatives of this generating function are then used to obtain moments of the distributions of interest.
